text: Listen to part of a talk in a neuroscience class.
script: W: Today I want to look at a question neuroscientists still argue about: do adult human brains keep making new neurons? For most of the twentieth century, the textbook answer was no. You were born with all the neurons you'd ever have.

W: That view began to crack in the nineteen sixties, when researchers found new neurons forming in the hippocampus of adult rats, and later in songbirds and monkeys. The hippocampus, remember, is important for forming new memories.
W: Then, in the late nineteen nineties, a study of human brain tissue found signs of new cells in the adult hippocampus too. Many people took that as settling the matter.

W: But it didn't. In two thousand eighteen, one team examined human brain samples and reported that new neurons became extremely rare after childhood. That same year, another group looked at similar tissue and concluded that healthy older adults still produce them.

W: So how can two careful teams reach opposite conclusions? Part of the answer seems to be method. The markers used to spot young neurons can fade quickly after death, so how long the tissue waited before it was preserved may change what you see.

W: Some of my colleagues treat the question as closed, in one direction or the other. I'd say that's a bit premature. This is a measurement problem as much as a biological one, and until the methods improve, I'd keep both possibilities on the table.

text: Listen to part of a talk in an astronomy class.
script: M: Let's turn to a puzzle about spiral galaxies. If most of a galaxy's mass sits in its bright center, then stars far out near the edge should orbit more slowly, just as Neptune moves around the Sun much more slowly than Mercury does.

M: In the nineteen seventies, Vera Rubin and her colleagues measured how fast stars and gas were moving in the outer parts of galaxies. The speeds didn't drop off. The outer regions were moving about as fast as the inner ones.

M: The most popular explanation is dark matter: a large halo of matter we can't see, which adds extra gravity. Most astronomers accept it, partly because it also helps explain other observations, like the way galaxy clusters bend light.

M: There's a rival idea, though, called modified Newtonian dynamics. It says there's no hidden matter at all. Instead, gravity itself behaves a little differently when accelerations are extremely small, as they are at the edges of galaxies.

M: To be fair to that idea, it predicts the rotation of many individual galaxies remarkably well, sometimes better than dark matter models do. Where it struggles is on larger scales, with clusters of galaxies and the early universe.

M: And here's the awkward part for dark matter: decades of experiments built to detect its particles directly have found nothing so far. So the majority view is strong, but it isn't finished business.

explanation: The talk presents an observation, outer stars 'didn't drop off' in speed, and then two explanations: dark matter and modified Newtonian dynamics. Neptune and Mercury are only an example, and the option about detecting particles reverses the script, which says experiments 'have found nothing so far'.

text: Listen to part of a talk in a linguistics class.
script: W: The idea we're discussing today is linguistic relativity, the claim that the language you speak shapes the way you think. It's often linked to Benjamin Lee Whorf, who wrote about it in the nineteen thirties.

W: In its strong form, the claim is that language determines thought, so if your language lacks a word for something, you can't really think about it. Very few researchers accept that version today. People clearly grasp new concepts before they have words for them.
W: Whorf's own evidence also took a beating. He argued that the Hopi language had no way of talking about time, but later linguists showed that it has plenty of ways to do exactly that.

W: So is the whole idea dead? Not quite. A weaker version says language can nudge thinking, especially habits of attention. Take color. Russian has separate basic words for light blue and dark blue, and in experiments Russian speakers are slightly faster at telling those shades apart than English speakers are.
W: Notice how small that effect is, though. Russian speakers aren't seeing different colors. They're a fraction of a second quicker on one kind of task.
W: You'll find the strong version in popular articles all the time, usually under a dramatic headline. I'd just ask you to check which version the evidence actually supports before you repeat it.

text: Listen to part of a talk in a philosophy of science class.
script: M: Last week we asked what makes a theory scientific. Today, Karl Popper's answer. Popper said a theory is scientific if it's falsifiable, meaning it makes predictions that some possible observation could prove wrong.

M: His favorite example was Einstein. General relativity predicted that starlight would bend by a specific amount as it passed the Sun. In nineteen nineteen, astronomers checked during a solar eclipse. The theory could have failed. It didn't, and for Popper, that risk was exactly what made it science.

M: Critics, though, pointed out a problem. When a prediction fails, it's never just one theory on trial. You're also relying on your instruments, your background assumptions, and so on. So a failed prediction doesn't tell you which piece is wrong.

M: History gives a nice case. In the eighteen forties, Uranus wasn't moving the way Newton's laws said it should. Astronomers didn't throw out Newton. They assumed an unseen planet was pulling on it, calculated where it should be, and found Neptune.

M: So rescuing a theory can be perfectly good science. Then again, the same move failed with Mercury's orbit. A hidden planet was proposed there too, it was never found, and the real answer turned out to be Einstein's relativity.
M: Popper's idea is still useful as a rule of thumb, I think. But as a strict test of what counts as science, well, it's harder to apply than it first sounds.

To argue that Newton's laws were disproven by the discovery of Neptune
explanation: The professor gives 'Popper's answer', falsifiability, then says critics 'pointed out a problem' and ends by calling it 'harder to apply than it first sounds'. The planets are examples, and the Neptune case actually saved Newton's laws rather than disproving them.

text: Listen to part of a talk in an ecology class.
script: W: Today's topic is a hypothesis that ecology students meet early and then, increasingly, see questioned. It's called the intermediate disturbance hypothesis. A disturbance, in this sense, is anything that clears space: a storm, a fire, a flood, heavy grazing.

W: The idea goes like this. If disturbances are rare, a few strong competitors gradually take over and push everyone else out. If they're constant, only the hardiest, fastest-growing species survive. So the greatest variety of species should appear somewhere in the middle.

W: Classic support came from rocky shores. In one well-known study, boulders that waves overturned now and then held more kinds of seaweed than boulders that were rarely moved or rolled over all the time.

W: It's an elegant picture, and it found its way into conservation planning. But when researchers pulled together hundreds of studies, the predicted hump-shaped pattern showed up in only a minority of them. Often diversity simply rose, fell, or showed no clear pattern.

W: Some ecologists went further and argued that the hypothesis has a logic problem: disturbance on its own shouldn't let competitors live side by side in the long run unless other conditions are also met.
W: Its defenders say it still describes certain systems well. That may be so. But a rule that holds only some of the time is, let's say, a local story rather than a law of nature.

explanation: The professor introduces the intermediate disturbance hypothesis, gives its 'classic support', and then spends the rest of the talk on studies and arguments against it. Storms and seaweed are only examples, and conservation planning is mentioned once to show the idea's influence.

explanation: She introduces the boulders as 'classic support': rocks overturned 'now and then' had more kinds of seaweed than rocks rarely or constantly moved. That is the middle-level pattern the hypothesis predicts. Boulders rolled 'all the time' are only one group in the study, so the last option misses the point.

text: Listen to part of a talk in an economics class.
script: M: So, can you beat the stock market? The efficient market hypothesis, which became influential in the nineteen sixties and seventies, says, in its basic form, not reliably. The reasoning is that prices already reflect the information available to investors.

M: Think of it this way. If a company's good news were public and the price hadn't moved yet, traders would rush to buy, and the price would jump almost instantly. So by the time you read the news, the opportunity is gone.
M: There's real evidence behind this. Most professionally managed funds, once you subtract their fees, do worse over the long run than a simple fund that just tracks the whole market.

M: But behavioral economists have challenged the idea that markets are fully rational. They point to bubbles, like the rise and crash of internet company shares around the year two thousand, when prices drifted far above any sensible estimate of value. They also point to investors who hold on to losing shares too long and sell winners too early.
M: Defenders reply that spotting a bubble afterward is easy. Spotting it in advance, and profiting from that, is another matter entirely.

M: Interestingly, leading figures on both sides shared the Nobel Prize in economics in the same year, two thousand thirteen. Which tells you, perhaps, that the profession hasn't quite made up its mind.

explanation: The talk presents the efficient market hypothesis, that 'prices already reflect the information available', and then the behavioral economists' challenge. The first option reverses the hypothesis, which says by the time you read the news 'the opportunity is gone'.

text: Listen to part of a talk in an art history class.
script: W: In two thousand one, the painter David Hockney proposed something that upset a lot of art historians. Looking at European paintings from the early fourteen hundreds onward, he noticed a sudden jump in realism: folds of fabric, reflections on metal, the exact patterns of a carpet.
W: His explanation, developed with the physicist Charles Falco, was that some artists were using optical devices, curved mirrors or lenses, to project an image onto a surface and then paint from it.
W: The thesis has a certain appeal. Lenses and mirrors did exist at the time, and some details in these paintings, they argued, show the slight distortions you'd expect if a lens had been refocused.

W: Critics raised several objections. Almost no written record from the period describes artists working this way, which is odd for a method supposedly used so widely. Others tested the setups and found that images from early mirrors would have been dim and small, hard to work from.

W: And some critics took offense at what the thesis seemed to imply, that these painters' skill was a kind of trick. Hockney said that was never his point. A projected image, he argued, still has to be painted, and that takes enormous skill.

W: Personally, I find the question more interesting than any final answer. Even if the thesis turns out to be wrong, it's made a lot of people look much harder at how these paintings were actually made.

explanation: The professor describes Hockney and Falco's idea that artists used 'optical devices' to explain 'a sudden jump in realism', and then the objections to it. Hockney's own career is not discussed, and fabric and metal are only examples of realistic details.

text: Listen to part of a talk in a geology class.
script: M: Around seven hundred million years ago, something strange happened to Earth's climate. Geologists have found deposits left by glaciers in rocks that, at the time, sat near the equator. We know their position from magnetic signals in the rocks, which record the latitude where they formed.

M: The boldest explanation is the snowball Earth hypothesis: the whole planet froze over, oceans included, from the poles to the tropics. Once ice covers enough of the surface, it reflects so much sunlight that the cooling feeds on itself.

M: But then how did Earth escape? The proposed answer is volcanoes. They kept releasing carbon dioxide, and with the oceans frozen, very little of that gas was being removed. Over millions of years it built up, until the greenhouse effect melted the ice.
M: Supporters point to unusual layers of carbonate rock lying directly on top of the glacial deposits, which fit a sudden, very warm aftermath.

M: Critics prefer what's called a slushball Earth, where a band of open water stayed near the equator. Their main argument is biological. Many simple organisms that needed sunlight survived this period, and it's hard to see how, if every ocean was sealed under thick ice.

M: Snowball supporters have answers: small patches of open water, thin ice in places. But notice that each answer moves the snowball a little closer to the slushball. The two camps may end up meeting somewhere in the middle.

explanation: The professor presents the snowball Earth hypothesis and the rival slushball view, then discusses how they relate. The magnetic signals show the rocks' latitude, not their age, so the first option mixes up a detail.

text: Listen to part of a talk in an anthropology class.
script: W: For much of the twentieth century, anthropologists argued about where modern humans came from. There were two main camps, and I want to walk you through how the argument was, well, partly resolved.

W: The first camp held the multiregional model. Early human populations spread out of Africa long ago and then evolved into modern humans in several regions at once, in Africa, Europe and Asia, with enough interbreeding between regions to keep them one species.

W: The second camp held the recent African origin model, often called Out of Africa. Modern humans evolved in Africa alone and then spread across the world, replacing older groups like the Neanderthals without mixing with them.

W: In the late nineteen eighties, genetic studies seemed to settle things in favor of Out of Africa. Living Africans show more genetic variety than any other population, which is what you'd expect from the oldest population, the one the others branched off from.

W: Then, in two thousand ten, scientists published a draft of the Neanderthal genome. And it turned out that most people whose ancestors come from outside Africa carry a small share of Neanderthal DNA, roughly one to two percent.
W: So there was mixing after all. Not much, but some. Neither side got exactly what it predicted.
W: Today, most researchers describe a mostly African origin with a little interbreeding along the way. Which is a good reminder that a debate framed as either-or sometimes ends with a messier answer.

explanation: The professor presents two models of where modern humans 'came from' and shows how genetic findings 'partly resolved' the argument. The first option mixes up two details: it was living Africans, not Neanderthals, who show the most genetic variety.

explanation: She says 'living Africans show more genetic variety than any other population', as expected of 'the oldest population'. The first option reverses a later finding: Neanderthal DNA is found in people whose ancestors come from outside Africa.

text: Listen to part of a talk in a history of engineering class.
script: M: Some Roman harbor walls have been sitting in seawater for about two thousand years, and they're still standing. Modern concrete in the same conditions can start breaking down within decades. So what did the Romans know that we've, well, apparently forgotten?

M: One long-standing explanation focuses on volcanic ash. Roman builders mixed lime with ash from the area around the Bay of Naples, and ancient writers, including Vitruvius, praised this material for hardening even underwater.

M: In the twenty tens, researchers studying samples of harbor concrete found that seawater slowly seeping through it had caused rare minerals to grow in its cracks and pores. In other words, the material kept strengthening over time instead of just wearing away.
M: Then, in two thousand twenty-three, another team proposed a second factor. Roman concrete contains small white lumps of lime, which had long been dismissed as a sign of careless mixing.

M: The team argued that the lumps came from mixing with quicklime, which heats up as it reacts. When a crack forms and water gets in, the lumps can dissolve and refill the crack. A kind of self-healing.
M: Now, these explanations aren't really competitors. One is about structures in seawater, the other about cracks in general. They could both be true.

M: What strikes me is the second one. Something experts had written off as sloppy work might turn out to be deliberate technique. That's worth remembering whenever we judge old methods by modern standards.

explanation: The professor asks 'what did the Romans know' and then gives two explanations for the long life of Roman concrete: volcanic ash with seawater, and self-healing lime lumps. He never says modern engineers have copied these methods.

text: Listen to part of a talk in a neuroscience class.
script: W: In the nineteen nineties, a research group in Italy recording from single neurons in monkeys noticed something surprising. Certain cells in a motor area of the brain fired when a monkey grasped an object, and also when it simply watched someone else grasp one.

text: Listen to part of a talk in a linguistics class.
script: M: Children learn their first language remarkably fast, and mostly without formal teaching. The question is how. One influential answer comes from Noam Chomsky, whose work from the late nineteen fifties onward changed the field.

M: Chomsky's argument is often called the poverty of the stimulus. The language children hear, he said, is too limited and too messy to teach them all the rules they end up knowing. M: The rival view is usually called usage-based or statistical learning. It says children are extraordinary pattern detectors, and the input is much richer than Chomsky assumed.

M: A famous experiment from nineteen ninety-six supports this. Eight-month-old babies listened to a stream of made-up syllables for just two minutes. M: Now, the nativist side replies that finding words is one thing, but learning abstract grammar is a much bigger leap.
M: And that's fair. The baby study doesn't settle the grammar question.

M: Still, notice the direction of the research. Decade after decade, we keep finding that children can learn more from what they hear than anyone expected. That doesn't prove nothing is built in, but it does shrink how much needs to be.

text: Listen to part of a talk in a philosophy of science class.
script: W: Here's a question that sounds simple: when a scientific theory works, should we believe that the things it describes are real? Electrons, say, or genes before anyone could see them. Philosophers who say yes are called scientific realists.

W: Their strongest argument is sometimes called the no miracles argument. Our best theories make astonishingly precise predictions. If they weren't at least roughly true, that success would be a miracle, and nobody likes explaining things with miracles.

W: The opposing camp, the anti-realists, has a historical reply. Look at theories that were once extremely successful and are now abandoned. For much of the nineteenth century, physicists explained light as waves traveling through an invisible substance called the ether. That theory made excellent predictions. And there's no ether.
W: So, the argument goes, if past successful theories turned out false, why expect our current ones to be different? Philosophers call this the pessimistic induction.

W: Realists have tried to soften the blow. Some argue that what survives from old theories is their mathematical structure, even when the objects they described don't. Many of the equations for light waves, for example, were kept.
W: I find that move clever, though I notice it gives up quite a bit. If what we can trust is the structure and not the things, then the realist is believing less than she started out believing.

text: Listen to part of a talk in an ecology class.
script: M: In nineteen ninety-five, wolves were brought back to Yellowstone National Park after being absent for about seventy years. What happened next became one of the most famous stories in ecology.

M: A chain like this, predator to prey to plants, is called a trophic cascade. And the fear effect, elk changing where they go, is sometimes called the landscape of fear.

M: More recent research, though, has made the story more complicated. Some field studies that tracked elk with collars found that elk didn't avoid risky places nearly as strongly as the original accounts suggested.
M: Other things were changing at the same time. Bears and cougars were taking more elk calves, people were hunting elk outside the park, and a run of dry years affected plant growth.
M: And along some streams, willows haven't recovered much at all, partly because, without beavers and their dams, the water table dropped and the soil dried out.
M: So did wolves matter? Almost certainly. But the tidy version, where one animal restores a whole landscape, probably gives the wolves more credit than any single species deserves.

text: Listen to part of a talk in an economics class.
script: W: In nineteen fifty-eight, the economist Bill Phillips published a study of British data covering nearly a century. He found that when unemployment was low, wages tended to rise quickly, and when unemployment was high, wages rose slowly.

W: Other economists soon turned this into a relationship between unemployment and inflation, which became known as the Phillips curve. Policymakers read it almost as a menu. Accept a bit more inflation, and you could buy lower unemployment.

W: In the late nineteen sixties, Milton Friedman and Edmund Phelps argued that this menu wouldn't last. Their point was about expectations. If workers and businesses come to expect higher inflation, they build it into wages and prices, and then the extra inflation stops buying any extra jobs.

W: The nineteen seventies seemed to prove them right. Many countries had high inflation and high unemployment at the same time, something the simple curve said shouldn't happen. People called it stagflation.

W: Economists didn't throw the curve away, though. They rebuilt it with expectations included. In the newer version there's a short-run trade-off, but in the long run unemployment returns to a natural level, whatever the inflation rate.

W: And more recently the curve has puzzled people again. In several countries, unemployment fell very low in the years before twenty twenty without much rise in inflation, and economists still debate why.
W: So this history isn't really a theory being refuted. It's a theory being repaired, more than once, and maybe not for the last time.

script: W: When you picture ancient Greek sculpture, you probably imagine gleaming white marble. That image shaped centuries of European art. W: Some scholars have made full-color reconstructions, and you may have seen them in exhibitions: bright blues and reds, patterned clothing. Visitors are often shocked. Some find them garish, even a little cartoonish.

W: In other words, the reconstructions may be wrong in their details, but the basic point, that the statues were colored, isn't really in doubt.

text: Listen to part of a talk in a geology class.
script: M: In nineteen twelve, a German scientist named Alfred Wegener proposed that the continents had once been joined together and had slowly drifted apart. He called the ancient supercontinent Pangaea.

M: His evidence was actually pretty good. The coastlines of South America and Africa fit together like puzzle pieces. Fossils of the same land animals and plants appear on continents now separated by oceans. And rock layers and signs of ancient glaciers line up across those oceans too.

M: Yet most geologists, especially in Britain and North America, rejected the idea for decades. Why? The main objection was the mechanism. Wegener couldn't explain what force could push whole continents through the solid ocean floor, and physicists showed that the forces he suggested were far too weak.

M: It's tempting to call the critics stubborn, but put yourself in their place. A theory with no workable mechanism, proposed by someone who wasn't trained as a geologist. Skepticism wasn't unreasonable.

M: What changed things was the ocean floor itself. In the nineteen fifties and sixties, surveys revealed long underwater mountain ridges, with magnetic stripes in the rock on either side that matched like mirror images. New sea floor was forming at the ridges and spreading outward.
M: That gave a mechanism. Continents don't plow through the ocean floor. They ride along on moving plates.
M: So Wegener was right about drift but wrong about how it worked. And the theory that won, plate tectonics, kept his conclusion while throwing out his explanation.

text: Listen to part of a talk in an anthropology class.
script: W: Why did people start farming? It's not as obvious as it sounds. Studies of skeletons suggest that many early farmers were shorter and had more dental problems than the hunter-gatherers before them. Farming meant harder work and a narrower diet. So what pushed people into it?

text: Listen to part of a talk in a history of engineering class.
script: M: How did the ancient Egyptians lift millions of stone blocks to build the Great Pyramid at Giza? Most researchers agree ramps were involved. The argument is about what kind.

M: A second idea is a ramp spiraling around the outside of the pyramid. That's shorter, but it would have covered the corners and edges, which the builders needed to see to keep the shape accurate.

M: About twenty years ago, an architect proposed something bolder: a ramp inside the pyramid, spiraling up just beneath the surface. It's clever and solves both problems, but there's little direct physical evidence for it, and many Egyptologists remain unconvinced.

text: Listen to part of a talk in a neuroscience class.
script: M: Today's topic is a strange experience reported by many people who have lost an arm or a leg. Even years later, they may still feel the missing limb. It itches, it feels cold, and sometimes it even hurts. This is called a phantom limb.

text: Listen to part of a talk in an economics class.
script: M: Today's idea comes from the economist David Ricardo, who wrote about it in eighteen seventeen. It's called comparative advantage, and it explains why trade can benefit both sides, even when one side is better at everything.
M: Let's start with a simple example. Imagine a lawyer who is also the fastest typist in town. She types faster than her assistant. So should she do all her own typing?

M: Probably not. Every hour she spends typing is an hour she isn't working as a lawyer, which pays much more. Economists call what you give up the opportunity cost, and for her, the opportunity cost of typing is very high.

M: Her assistant types more slowly, but his opportunity cost is much lower, because he isn't giving up legal work. So it makes sense for him to type and for her to practice law. Together, they get more done.

M: Ricardo applied the same logic to countries. His example was England and Portugal, cloth and wine. Even if Portugal could produce both more efficiently, both countries could gain if each focused on the good it gave up the least to produce, and then traded.
M: Notice the key word: comparative, not absolute. What matters isn't who's best at something, but who gives up the least to do it.
M: Real trade is more complicated, of course. Some workers and industries can lose out, even when a country gains overall. But the basic idea remains one of the most important in economics.

script: M: You may have heard the claim that humans can maintain only about a hundred and fifty meaningful relationships. That's Dunbar's number, proposed in the early nineteen nineties by the anthropologist Robin Dunbar.

M: The reasoning behind it is clever. Among monkeys and apes, species with a larger neocortex, the outer layer of the brain, tend to live in larger social groups. M: Critics also note that human social life depends heavily on culture, language and technology, not just brain size, so a prediction based on other primates may not transfer well.

text: Listen to part of a talk in a history of engineering class.
script: W: For centuries, sailors could work out their latitude, how far north or south they were, fairly easily from the height of the Sun or certain stars. Longitude, their east-west position, was far harder, and errors could leave a ship badly off course.

W: The principle was understood. Earth turns fifteen degrees every hour. So if you know the local time on your ship and, at the same moment, the time at your home port, the difference gives your longitude. The problem was knowing the home port time at sea.
W: In seventeen fourteen, the British government offered a large prize for a practical solution, and two very different approaches competed.

W: Astronomers favored the lunar distance method. By measuring the angle between the Moon and a particular star, and checking printed tables, a navigator could work out the home port time. It needed accurate tables and long calculations, but no costly equipment.

W: The other approach was to carry the home port time with you in a clock. Most experts doubted any clock could stay accurate on a rolling ship. But a self-taught clockmaker, John Harrison, spent decades proving them wrong, and his sea watch performed remarkably well on trial voyages in the seventeen sixties.
W: What the heroic story often leaves out is that these clocks stayed expensive for decades, so many ships kept using lunar distances well into the eighteen hundreds.
W: So the experts' preference for astronomy wasn't just snobbery. For a long time, it was the method most ships could actually afford.

text: Listen to part of a talk in an ecology class.
script: M: In the nineteen seventies, the scientist James Lovelock, working with the biologist Lynn Margulis, proposed what he called the Gaia hypothesis, named after a Greek goddess of the Earth. The claim was that living things and their surroundings form a self-regulating system that keeps conditions on Earth suitable for life.

M: Lovelock pointed to some striking facts. The amount of oxygen in the air has stayed fairly stable for hundreds of millions of years. And although the Sun has grown brighter over Earth's history, the surface has stayed within a range where liquid water can exist.

M: Biologists were quick to object. Natural selection acts on individual organisms and their genes. So how could countless separate organisms end up regulating a whole planet? It sounded as if life were planning ahead, which evolution doesn't do.

M: Lovelock answered with a computer model called Daisyworld, a planet with only dark and light daisies. Dark daisies absorb heat and light ones reflect it. As the sun warms, the balance between them shifts, and the temperature stays fairly steady, without any daisy aiming for that.
M: The model persuaded some critics that regulation without planning was possible in principle. Whether Earth actually works that way is another question.

M: Today, the strong version of Gaia has few supporters. But the broader idea, that life and the physical planet shape each other, has become central to what's now called Earth system science. So a hypothesis can be largely rejected and still leave a lasting mark.
